<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|British|688|broad}}</noinclude>of the ancient Britons, represented by the modern Welsh and Cornish.

'''Britisher''' (brit′ish-ėr), ''n.'' A British subject or citizen in any part of the world, but more particularly a native or an inhabitant of Great Britain, especially of England. [Now chiefly colloquial or humorous.]

'''Briton''' (brit′on), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< ME. ''Britun, Brutun'', etc., < OF. ''Breton'', a Briton, usually a Breton or native of Brittany in France, < ML. ''Brito(n-)'', pl. ''Britones'', L. ''Britanni'', Britons: see ''British''.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' A native of Great Britain; especially, one of the original Celtic inhabitants of the island of Britain.

'''II.''' ''a.'' British. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|A ''Briton'' peasant.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 1.}}}}

'''britska''' (brits′kä), ''n.''   [Also written ''britzska'' and, more prop., ''britchka''; < Pol. ''bryczka'' = Russ. ''brichka'', dim. of Pol. ''bryka'', a freight-wagon, = Russ. ''brikŭ'', a sort of light carriage.]   In Russia, a light, partly covered four-wheeled carriage. {{smaller|The Polish britska, also used in Russia, has a pole, a body of wickerwork, and a leather top.}}

'''britt<sup>1</sup>, britt<sup>2</sup>.''' See ''brit<sup>1</sup>'', ''brit<sup>2</sup>''.

'''britten†''' (brit′n), ''v. t.''   [E. dial., < ME. ''brittenen, britnen, bryttenen, bruttenen, brutnen, bretnen'', divide, break up, cut to pieces, < AS. ''brytnian'', divide, distribute, dispense (cf. Icel. ''brotna'', be broken), < ''breótan'' (pp. *''broten''), break: see ''brit<sup>1</sup>''.]   To break up; cut to pieces; cut up; carve.
{{smaller block|Thus schall I ''brittyn'' all youre bones on brede.
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 292.}}}}

'''britterworts''' (brit′ėr-wėrts), ''n. pl.'' The ''Diatomaceæ.''

'''brittle''' (brit′l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''britel, brutel, brotel,'' etc., < AS. as if *''brytel,'' with suffix ''-el'' forming adjectives from verbs, < ''breótan'' (pret. ''breát,'' pl. *''bruton,'' pp. *''broten''), break: see ''brit''<sup>1</sup> and ''britten.'' Cf. ''brickle,'' an equiv. word of different origin.]   '''1†.''' Fickle; changeable.
{{smaller block|How ''brotel'' and how false he was.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 2555.}}}}
'''2.''' Breaking easily and suddenly with a comparatively smooth fracture, as glass; fragile; not tough or tenacious.
{{smaller block|Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, . . . becomes ''brittle'' at temperatures approaching to redness, but while cold it possesses considerable malleability.
{{right|''W. A. Miller'', Elem. of Chem., § 519.}}}}
'''3.''' Figuratively, easily destroyed; perishable; fleeting.
{{smaller block|<poem>One woful day sweeps children, friends and wife,
And all the ''brittle'' blessings of my life!</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Lucretius, iii. 85.}}}}
'''Brittle silver ore.''' {{smaller|Same as ''stephanite.''}}

'''brittleness''' (brit′l-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brittilnesse, brutelnes,'' etc.]   '''1†.''' Instability; changeableness.
{{smaller block|<poem>The see may ebbe and flowe more and lesse,
The welken hath might to shyne, reyne and hayle:
Right so mote I kythe my ''brotelnesse.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Fortune, l. 63.}}}}
'''2.''' The property of breaking readily with a comparatively smooth fracture; frangibility: the opposite of ''toughness'' and ''tenacity.''
{{smaller block|A rod of good steel, in its hardest state, is broken almost as easily as a rod of glass of the same size, and this ''brittleness'' can only be diminished by diminishing its hardness.
{{right|''G. Ede'', in Campin’s Mech. Engineering, p. 360.}}}}

'''brittle-star''' (brit′l-stär), ''n.'' A name of sundry sand-stars, or ophiurians, from their fragility. See cuts under ''Astrophyton'' and ''star-fish''.

'''britzska''', ''n.'' See ''britska''.

'''Briza''' (brī′zä̤), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. βρίζειν, nod (cf. the common name ''quaking-grass''). The form seems to have been suggested by Gr. βρίζα, a grain like rye, in Thrace and Macedonia still so called. Cf. Æolic βρίσδα, for ῥίζα, root.]   A genus of grasses, commonly called quaking-grass, maidenhair-grass, or lady’s-hair. {{smaller|There are ten species, mostly natives of Europe and the Mediterranean region, of little agricultural importance. Some of them are cultivated for ornament on account of their gracefully nodding spikes.}}

'''brize<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''breeze''<sup>1</sup>.

'''brize<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''breeze''<sup>2</sup>.

'''brize<sup>3</sup>''', ''n.'' See ''brise''<sup>3</sup>.

'''brizé''' (brē-zā′), ''a.'' Same as ''brisé''.

'''brizure''' (briz′ụ̄r), ''n.'' Same as ''brisure'', 1.

'''bro.''' An abbreviation of ''brother''; pl. ''bros.'': as, Smith ''Bros.'' & Co.

'''broach''' (brōch), ''n.''   [Also, in sense of an ornamental pin, spelled ''brooch'' (see ''brooch''<sup>1</sup>); early mod. E. ''broche'', < ME. ''broche'', a pin, peg, spit, spear-point, taper, < OF. ''broche'', F. ''broche'', a spit, brooch, etc., = Pr. ''broca'' = Sp. Pg. ''broca'', an awl, drill, spool, etc., = It. ''brocca'', a split stick (with masculine forms, OF. and F. dial. ''broc'', a spit, = It. ''brocco'', a sharp stake, a sprout, etc.), < ML. ''broca'', ''brocca'', a spit, a sharp stake, any sharp-pointed thing; cf. L. ''brochus'', ''brocchus'', ''brocus'', projecting (of the teeth of animals: see ''brochate''); prob. of Celtic origin: cf. W. ''procio'', stab, prick (> E. ''prog''); Gael. ''brog'', a shoemakers’ awl, < ''brog'', spur, stimulate, goad (> E. ''brog''<sup>1</sup>).]   '''1†.''' A spit.
{{smaller block|Thre balefulle birdez his ''brochez'' they turne.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'', l. 1029.}}}}
{{smaller block|And some failed not to take the child and bind it to a ''broach'', and lay it to the fire to roast.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 259.}}}}
{{smaller block|He turned a ''broach'', that had worn a crown.
{{right|''Bacon'', Hist. Hen. VII.}}}}
'''2†.''' A spear.
{{smaller block|<poem>That fruit was of a mayden born
On a theoues tre is al totorn
A ''broche'' thorwout his brest [bor]n.</poem>
{{right|''Legends of the Holy Rood'' (ed. Morris), p. 133.}}}}
'''3.''' An awl; a bodkin. [Prov. Eng.]—'''4.''' A spike; a skewer; a sharp stick; specifically, a rod of sallow, hazel, or other tough and pliant wood, sharpened at each end and bent in the middle, used by thatchers to pierce and fix their work. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|''Broche'' for a thacstare [thaxter, thatcher], firmaculum.
{{right|''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 52.}}}}
'''5†.''' A spur.—'''6†.''' A fish-hook.   ''Prompt. Parv.''—'''7†.''' A spike or standard for a candle.
{{smaller block|A ''broche'' with a fote, ij new torches.
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 327.}}}}
'''8†.''' A taper; a torch.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hewe fuyr of a flynt four hundred wynter;
Bote thou haue tache to take hit with tunder and ''broches''.</poem> Al thy labour is lost.{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xx. 211.}}}}
'''9.''' A spindle; a spool. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|''Broche'' of threde, vericulum.{{right|''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 52.}}}}
'''10.''' In ''arch.'', formerly, a spire of any kind; now, specifically, as used in some parts of England {{img float|file=century v01 p0714 c2f1.png|width=232px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Broaches.}} {{smaller|''A'', southwest tower, Cathedral of Bayeux, Normandy;   ''B'', Church of St. Nicholas, Walcot, England.}}}} and by some writers on architecture, a spire which rises directly from the walls of its tower, without parapets and gutters. —'''11.''' A narrow-pointed chisel used by masons for hewing stones. —'''12.''' Any tapered boring-bit or drill. {{smaller|Broaches used for boring wood are fluted like the shell-bit, but tapered toward the point; but those used in boring metal are solid, and usually three-, four-, or six-sided. Their common forms are shown in the annexed figures. Broaches are also known as ''wideners'' and ''reamers''.}} '''13.''' A straight steel tool with file-teeth for pressing through irregular holes in metal that {{img float|file=century v01 p0714 c2f2.png|width=127px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Broaches for Boring. Fig. ''a'' is an example of broaches or reamers for wood, and fig. ''b'' of those for metal.}}}} cannot be dressed by revolving tools.—'''14.''' That part of the stem of a key which projects beyond the bit or web, and enters a socket in the interior of the lock.—'''15.''' That pin in a lock which enters the barrel of the key.   ''E. H. Knight.''—'''16.''' The stick from which candle-wicks are suspended for dipping.—'''17.''' A gimlet used in opening casks for sampling their contents.—'''18.''' A fitting for an Argand gas-burner.—'''19.''' A start, like the end of a spit, on the head of a young stag.—'''20.''' A pin or clasp to fasten a garment; specifically, an ornamental pin, clasp, or buckle, and especially a breastpin, of gold, silver, or other metal, attached to the dress or depending from the neck: in this sense now usually spelled ''brooch'' (which see).

'''broach''' (brōch), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''brochen'', bore, spur, spit, tap (in this sense cf. the phrase ''setten on broche'', set abroach, after F. ''mettre en broche:'' see ''abroach''), < OF. ''brocher'', spur, spit, etc., F. ''brocher'', stitch, figure, emboss (= Pr. ''brocar'' = Pg. ''brocar'', bore, = It. ''broccare'', urge, incite, etc.), < ''broche'', etc., spit: see ''broach'', ''n.'' Cf. ''brocade'', ''brochure'', etc.]   '''1†.''' To spit; pierce as with a spit.
{{smaller block|The Erle that knew & wyst moche of the chasse ''broched'' the bore thrughe the brest.
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 235, note.}}}}
{{smaller block|I’ll ''broach'' the tadpole on my rapier’s point.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iv. 2.}}}}
'''2†.''' To spur.
{{smaller block|''Brocheȝ'' the baye stede, and to the buske rydeȝ.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 918.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''masonry'', to rough-hew. [North. Eng. and Scotch.]—'''4.''' To open for the first time for the purpose of taking out something; more especially, to tap or pierce, as a cask in order to draw the liquor: as, to ''broach'' a hogshead.
{{smaller block|Descending into the cellars, they ''broached'' every cask they found there.
{{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, I. 564.}}}}
Hence, figuratively—'''5.''' To open, as the mouth for utterance.
{{smaller block|<poem>Desiring Virtue might be her first growth,
And Hallelujah ''broach'' her holy mouth.</poem>
{{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, i. 68.}}}}
'''6.''' To let out; shed.
{{smaller block|This blow should ''broach'' thy dearest blood.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., iii. 4.}}}}
'''7.''' To state or give expression to for the first time; utter; give out; especially, begin conversation or discussion about; introduce by way of topic: as, to ''broach'' a theory or an opinion.
{{smaller block|This error . . . was first ''broached'' by Josephus.
{{right|''Raleigh'', Hist. World, i. 3.}}}}
<poem>Here was our Paolo brought
To ''broach'' a weighty business.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, I. 107.}}}}

'''8†.''' To give a start to; set going.
{{smaller block|That for her love such quarrels may be ''broach’d.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., ii. 1.}}}}

'''Droved and broached.''' {{smaller|See ''drove''<sup>3</sup>.}}—'''To broach to''' {{smaller|(''naut.'', used intransitively), to come suddenly to the wind, as a ship, by accident or by the fault of the helmsman (a dangerous position in a gale).}}

'''broacher''' (brō′chėr), ''n.''   [< ''broach'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' A spit.
{{smaller block|On five sharp ''broachers'' rank’d the roast they turn’d.
{{right|''Dryden'', Iliad, i. 638.}}}}
'''2.''' One who broaches, opens, or utters; a first publisher.
{{smaller block|The first ''broacher'' of a heretical opinion.
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Deadly haters of truth, ''broachers'' of lies.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., iii.}}}}

'''broaching-press''' (brō′ching-pres), ''n.'' A machine-tool employing a broach, used in slotting and finishing iron.

'''broach-post''' (brōch′pōst), ''n.'' In ''carp.'', a king-post.

'''broach-turner''' (brōch′tėr″nėr), ''n.'' A menial whose occupation is to turn a broach or spit; a turnspit.
{{smaller block|<poem>Dish-washer and ''broach-turner'', loon!—to me
Thou smellest all of kitchen as before.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Gareth and Lynette.}}}}

'''broad''' (brâd), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [= Sc. ''braid''; < ME. ''brood'', ''brod'', < AS. ''brād'' = OS. ''brēd'' = OFries. ''brēd'' = D. ''breed'' = MLG. ''brēd'', LG. ''breed'' = OHG. MHG. G. ''breit'' = Icel. ''breidhr'' = Sw. Dan. ''bred'' = Goth. ''braids'', broad. Hence ''bread''<sup>2</sup>, ''breadth''. The pron. would be reg. brōd (like ''goad'', ''road'', etc.).]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Wide; having great breadth, as distinguished from length and thickness; used absolutely, having much width or breadth; not narrow: as, a strip no ''broader'' than one’s hand; a ''broad'' river or street.
{{smaller block|In are [a] ''brode'' strete he igon mete threo cnihtes.
{{right|''Layamon'', I. 217.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Broad'' breast, full eye, small head, and nostril wide.
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 296.}}}}
'''2.''' Large superficially; extensive; vast: as, the ''broad'' expanse of ocean.
{{smaller block|<poem>Each year shall give this apple-tree
A ''broader'' flush of roseate bloom.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Planting of the Apple-Tree.}}}}
'''3.''' Figuratively, not limited or narrow; liberal; comprehensive; enlarged: as, a man of ''broad'' views.
{{smaller block|In a ''broad'', statesmanlike, and masterly way. {{right|''Everett.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Narrow spirits admire basely and worship meanly; ''broad'' spirits worship the right. {{right|''Thackeray.''}}}}
Specifically—'''4.''' Inclined to the Broad Church, or to the views held by the Broad-Church party of the Church of England. See ''Episcopal.''—'''5.''' Large in measure or degree; not small or slight; ample; consummate.
{{smaller block|ʒif hym-self be bore blynde hit is a ''brod'' wonder.
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 584.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
